catalog_quote: Brown 1968: 'He also introduced various other diacritical marks, such as lea, to distinguish it from lea', which has a final stress. To distinguish some of the personal pronouns from other words having the same spelling but a penultimate stress, he employed accents, ara 'I', ara 'far'; are 'he''she''it' are 'new'; ela 'we' (exclus.) ela 'strong'; ere 'they', ere 'belly. ... The stress is generally on the penultimate syllable. Notable exceptions are some of the pronouns. These have accent marks, as has already been stated, inorder to indicate stress. In the case of other exceptions the stress pattern is given.' Brown 1986: 'In both Orokolo and Toaripi, with words of two or three syllables, the stress is normally on the penultimate syllable. audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding quotations (Brown 1968 Orthography preface; Brown 1986 p. xiv 'Stress') are present verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated places. (2) The cited deciding source is a dictionary preface, but the classification is independently confirmed by the best published description, Brown 1973 PL C-26 section 8.15.1 'Stress' p. 307, which we hold (our earlier reading) and which I read: penultimate primary stress 'usually', lexical exceptions (nominative pronouns ara/are/ela/ere with final stress, faitora 'now', pitoo), stress normalises to penult under suffixation (-ro, -ve), minor stress two syllables left of the penult in 4+ syllable words (karikara /kàrikára/), compounds follow the same pattern, reduplications repeat stem stress, onomatopoeics may reverse. sources.note: Word-level penultimate stress as the general rule; lexical exceptions: some personal pronouns (ara 'I', are 'he/she/it', ela 'we excl.', ere 'they') carry a non-penultimate stress marked by an accent, lea' has final stress, and the converb forms a', la', sa' carry the same mark; other exceptions have their stress pattern given in the entries. sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1907. A Grammar of the Toaripi Language spoken at the Eastern end of the Gulf of Papua. In Reports of the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition to Torres Straits, vol. III: Linguistics, pp. 333-346. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
sources.quote: None. The Phonology section lists vowels, consonants, Holmes's notes on vowel combinations, l/r and m/v interchange, and 'All syllables end in a vowel'; no mention of accent or stress anywhere in the Toaripi grammar (a full-text search for stress/accent pp. 333-346 for accent/stress/emphasis finds only 'emphasise the meaning' in a syntax note).
